newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Spot Products-Prices slide as NYMEX weakens.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Spot Products-Prices slide as NYMEX weakens.

text.p: U.S. Gulf conventional gasoline differentials gained modestly Wednesday, aided by problems at Lyondell's Houston, Texas refinery.

However, outright prices weakened as the NYMEX basis prices fell sharply. July gasoline futures shed 1.70 cents to end at 56.78 cents a gallon and July heating oil dropped 1.01 cents to settle at 51.44 cents a gallon.
U.S. GULF
Prompt regular conventional southern-grade M1 gasoline changed hands as high as 3.25 cents under the July NYMEX, up about 0.25 cent from late Tuesday levels.
Market watchers said increased buying interest emerged after shut a 96,000 barrel-per-day catalytic cracker. The company said the unit was shut briefly Tuesday but had been restarted.
However, traders said its was not likely that the unit had been restarted so quickly.
Prompt conventional 93-octane premium gasoline traded at 6.00 cents over the prompt M1 gasoline, up more than 0.50 cent on the day.
Players said distillate differentials sat nearly unchanged from the previous day, though 54-grade jet fuel traded at 0.15 cent over the July futures, up from about even with the screen on Tuesday.
MIDCONTINENT

Chicago market unleaded gasoline differentials remained weak Wednesday after falling earlier in the day on selling by a few refiners, traders said. With second cycle nearly over, most players were quoting third cycles barrels at 1.00/1.25 over the July NYMEX. The value is about a penny below Tuesday.
Group Three unleaded differentials also held onto lower values in quiet trade. Prompt barrels were pegged 3.50/3.75 cents to the print. Any months were 3.00/3.25 cents.
"BP and a few other refiners came out selling and there wasn't much demand so the market collapsed," said a Chicago player.
Low sulphur diesel in both hubs were quiet amid little activity.
NEW YORK HARBOR
New York Harbor refined product markets were on the quiet side Wednesday afternoon, with weakening differentials on "D2" northern grade 93-octane premium gasoline to show for it.

Action on distillates was a bit more lively, as buyers continued to take advantage of the attractive contango on the screen and sock barrels away ahead of the autumn and winter seasons of high distillate consumption.
Traders said prompt D2 premium gasoline got done at 7.50 cents over July futures -- off 0.50 cent from the levels seen late last week and early this week.
Traders have been doubting differentials on D2 of 8.00 for the last few sessions, but it took a weaker deal to make those doubts reality.

Prompt "A2" regular reformulated northern grade gasoline got done at 0.25 cent under the screen -- unchanged from Tuesday's levels, but buyers appeared to be hiding in the grass waiting for deals at weaker levels.
"It was hard to get anything done. There were a lot more sellers than buyers," said one trader, referring to the A2 grade.
The regular conventional "M2" northern grade weakened a touch amid the thinness and concerns of oversupply, with prompt barrels getting done at 2.75 and 2.80 cents under July NYMEX.
Players were looking across the Atlantic wondering if imports were going to add to the growing sense that record supplies are increasingly overwhelming what appears to be solid demand.

But the trans-Atlantic gasoline arbitrage window remained closed, and some were talking about the possibility of some Northwest Europe supplies heading down to the Mediterranean, which will limit the bearish pressure on gasoline prices in the U.S.

On the distillate front, prompt barrels of heating oil repeatedly traded at the price of July futures with players snatching up supplies to take advantage of the 4.46 cents contango between the July 1997 and January 1998 heating oil contracts on the NYMEX.

"That's really pretty good," said one player referring to the carry, and noting that for some, the carry would be attractive enough at 2.50 to think about storing supplies in tankage ahead of the winter.
